When a request comes in, the operator’s job is basically: validate inputs → figure out what systems it needs → check readiness/limits → compute the smallest safe set of actions → run what it can without approval → route anything risky through your approval.

What it checks first
- The request shape: what exact action you want (create vs update vs send vs label/archive), and what target it needs (record, contact, thread, workspace, etc.).
- The required fields: whether it has enough concrete data to execute without guessing (emails, IDs, mappings, audience).
- The connector readiness: whether the relevant integrations for reads/writes are connected and authenticated. (If a connector isn’t connected, it stops and asks for the missing connection rather than trying to proceed.)

How it decides if approval is needed
- Anything that mutates external systems (especially writes) is treated as approval-gated unless the platform explicitly says it’s safe to run without approval.
- It also gates when the operation could cause irreversible or high-impact outcomes, like sending emails, changing pipeline/CRM records broadly, archiving data, or touching large batches.
- If the operator would have to make an assumption that changes meaning (wrong target, ambiguous time window, unclear recipient set), it routes to approval by default—or asks a clarifying question before proceeding.

How it executes safely (the “operator loop”)
- Plan the minimal action set: read what it needs, then apply only the necessary writes.
- Dry-run mentally / simulate constraints: confirm there’s no missing critical field and that the action matches your intent (send vs draft vs label change, etc.).
- Run the writes only when all required prerequisites are satisfied; otherwise it stops at the first blocker with the exact missing detail.

One thing I’ll flag: I don’t have your exact platform’s internal policy wording in this chat (what counts as “approval-required” vs “auto-approved”). If you tell me what you consider high-risk (email sends? batch CRM updates? anything touching production data), I’ll describe the decision boundary in those terms.
